At 06:58 the city begins dimming itself.

Not dramatically. The streetlamps cool from white to amber. Transit platforms lower their announcement volume by six decibels. Coffee grinders in cafés pause mid-cycle, leaving hoppers half-full. Apartment mirrors cloud automatically if they detect more than one face nearby.

Mara notices all of it without looking up from her breakfast.

Two minutes to overlap.

The old people still call it “the spill,” though the official term has been Civic Synchronization Event. Nobody under forty says either. Most people just glance at clocks reflexively the way earlier centuries checked weather.

Her kettle clicks off. Outside her apartment window, cyclists coast instead of pedaling. A pair of schoolchildren stop arguing in perfect mutual instinct.

06:59:55.

The city exhales.

Five seconds arrive.

Not sound exactly. More intimate than sound. Thoughts emerge stripped of intention but carrying emotional texture intact, as if language itself had forgotten how to lie.

—forgot to send the money again—
—don’t think about blood don’t think about blood—
—her hand was warm this morning—
—I could jump—
—need eggs—
—please let him still love me—
—itching under the bandage—
—I hate this song—
—smile back at the child smile back—
—what if the diagnosis was wrong—

Then silence returns so abruptly it feels manufactured.

A bus resumes braking. Somewhere a spoon hits ceramic. The cyclists pedal on.

Mara checks the municipal dashboard on her kitchen wall. Green across all districts except the river quarter, where synchronization intensity has risen three percent above seasonal baseline. Probably exam stress from the university again.

She taps in a recommendation package: deploy additional drift musicians near tram corridors. Delay targeted advertising for two hours. Increase ambient water audio in public plazas.

Small corrections. Most of her work is small corrections.

People imagine silence engineers as psychologists with authority over emotion. In reality they are infrastructure workers. Urban maintenance for moments no one can prevent.

By 07:30 she’s underground in Maintenance Chamber C beneath Saint Ardin Station, inspecting resonance baffles.

The city learned centuries ago that architecture matters during overlap. Narrow stone corridors amplify panic thoughts. Glass atriums increase perceived loneliness by causing echoes of internal cadence. Curved ceilings soothe crowds by blending monologues into meaningless wash.

Nobody fully understands why.

There are theories involving predictive cognition and social threat assessment. Mara once dated a neuroscientist who insisted overlap trauma came from “forced unmasking of stochastic identity drift,” which sounded impressive and explained nothing.

What mattered was outcome. The old train tunnels, built before acoustic reforms, produced measurable spikes in depressive episodes. Parks reduced them. So did fountains, birds, and bakeries.

Especially bakeries.

The human mind, it turned out, tolerated hearing strangers think terrible things if the air smelled faintly of bread.

At 08:00 she stands with commuters on the platform.

People observe etiquette without acknowledging it. Eyes lower. Bodies angle away slightly. No one wants to be seen receiving another person’s thoughts.

Five seconds.

—his funeral tie smelled like dust—
—steal it steal it now—
—I’m so tired of performing kindness—
—her ears are beautiful—
—don’t let the baby stop breathing—
—I chose wrong twenty years ago—

The train arrives exactly as the overlap ends.

Timing is deliberate. Municipal transit schedules are built around emotional decompression windows. Riders need immediate procedural tasks after synchronization: boarding, scanning passes, finding seats. Simple decisions reduce fixation.

A teenager across from Mara quietly says, “Pretty rough one.”

No one answers. Another etiquette. You may acknowledge intensity but never content. Discussing specific overheard thoughts is considered a form of intimacy bordering on assault.

At City Hall Annex, Mara attends the weekly Harmonics Review.

“Commercial districts are requesting reduced hush intervals,” says Deputy Planner Venn, rubbing his temple. “Retail claims silence protocols suppress morning sales.”

“Of course they do,” Mara says. “That’s the point.”

A century ago corporations tried exploiting overlap psychologically. Synchronization sales tactics. Emotional priming. For a few catastrophic years advertisements were timed immediately after the spill, when citizens were cognitively raw and unusually suggestible.

The reforms afterward became foundational civic law.

No targeted messaging within fifteen minutes of overlap.
No political speeches within thirty.
No marriage proposals within sixty.

Especially not proposals.

The room’s oldest engineer, Kel, slides a report across the table. “Suicide clusters are down in the east wards since installation.”

Mara studies the figures. Rooftop gardens, sheltered benches, low-frequency wind chimes.

Tiny interventions against despair.

“What caused the improvement?” she asks.

Kel shrugs. “People feel less alone hearing terrible thoughts if they’re surrounded by growing things.”

That sounds simplistic. It is also probably true.

At noon the overlap catches Mara outside unexpectedly.

She’s crossing Republic Square when the clocks embedded in the tram wires pulse blue.

Five seconds.

—she recognized me from the trial—
—I want another child—
—everyone here is pretending—
—don’t turn around—
—maybe today I won’t go home—
—I miss my dog’s smell—
—what if consciousness is only embarrassment—

The square stills.

A little girl nearby squeezes her father’s hand afterward and asks, “Did somebody do a sad one?”

“Probably several,” he says gently.

Children adapt fastest. They grow up understanding that minds produce horrors continuously and usually harmlessly. Developmental psychologists say this prevents certain forms of narcissism. It also creates others.

Teenagers in Mara’s city rarely ask, “What’s wrong with me?”
They ask, “How well do I conceal what’s wrong with me during the other fifty-nine minutes?”

By evening rain moves through downtown, softening traffic noise into hiss.

Mara’s final inspection is at a residential complex requesting certification for overlap-safe communal housing. The architect proudly demonstrates staggered corridor curves, private decompression alcoves, and absorbent wall textiles.

“Residents report forty percent less post-spill anxiety,” he says.

A couple passes them carrying groceries. As they near the top of the stairs, the woman briefly reaches for the man’s sleeve, not affectionately exactly, but preemptively.

19:59.

Everyone in the building slows.

Mara watches faces enter that peculiar expressionless neutrality people learn young: not hiding emotion, just loosening attachment to being fully known.

Five seconds.

—leave me leave me leave me—
—I hope she never discovers—
—this soup again—
—I would die for him—
—I think I’m becoming my father—
—please survive the night—
—her laugh saved me—

Silence returns.

The couple continues upstairs.

Neither speaks, but their hands find each other again automatically, with the weary tenderness of people who understand that love is partly choosing which thoughts do not represent a person.

Outside, the rain thickens.

Mara walks home through streets engineered to absorb the human mind gently: softened corners, warm lighting, trees positioned not for beauty but for recovery. Above her, windows glow across thousands of apartments.

In fifty-three minutes the city will hear itself again.

Already, unconsciously, it is preparing.

The archive announced its own ending in increments of dimming light.

Along the central corridor, the ceiling panels lowered themselves from daylight white to the amber of late afternoon, though no sun had ever existed within three million kilometers of the structure. The adjustment was ceremonial, inherited from a species that had once believed conclusions should resemble evening.

Archivist Talan moved slowly beneath the fading lights with one hand resting against the warm metal wall. The climate systems had already begun their gradual reduction. Air no longer circulated with the same confidence. Dust, impossible for centuries, had gathered in the corners where the corridor ribs met the floor.

On either side stretched the rooms of the extinct.

Not tombs. The archive charter had forbidden that word. Tombs implied reverence for the dead. The archive had been built for continuity, for eventual rediscovery, for the assumption that somewhere intelligence persisted and would someday wish to know what had vanished before it.

No one had come in a very long time.

Talan paused beside Room 442-K. The door membrane recognized him after a slight delay, its ancient processors taking a moment to surface from dormancy. Inside, the preserved atmosphere carried the faint mineral scent of rain striking hot stone.

The civilization cataloged here had evolved beneath high gravity and perpetual storms. Their room contained no written language, no visual records. Memory, to them, had been acoustic pressure encoded inside columns of porous crystal. Along the walls stood hundreds of waist-high spires, pale blue and honeycombed.

Talan crossed to the nearest one and laid his fingertips lightly against its surface.

The crystal answered with a low vibration.

A city mourning ceremony unfolded through his bones rather than his ears. Dense rhythmic pulses traveled up his arm and into his chest cavity: thousands gathering silently under storm shelters while tectonic sirens sounded offshore. The emotional structure of the event was impossible to translate fully into humanoid cognition. Grief and civic pride were not distinct sensations to them. To lose someone was to become briefly more structurally complete as a community.

The archive notes had struggled with this for centuries.

Their art had worked similarly. Buildings were designed to resonate with weather patterns, producing harmonic distortions during hurricanes. Their greatest masterpieces existed only during disasters severe enough to destroy them.

Talan withdrew his hand.

The crystal slowly quieted.

There would be no one left to touch these records once the archive powered down. The thought no longer felt tragic exactly. Tragedy implied interruption. This was closer to erosion.

Back in the corridor, he continued toward the older sectors where the gravity fluctuated softly beneath the floor grilles. The archive had been expanded so many times that incompatible engineering philosophies overlapped awkwardly. Some halls preferred straight lines. Others bent almost imperceptibly to satisfy extinct mathematical aesthetics.

A maintenance drone passed overhead carrying coils of decommissioned fiber-optic vine. It did not acknowledge him. Most higher systems had already surrendered executive function in preparation for closure.

Room 811-A contained an atmosphere too thin for comfort. Frost feathered the interior observation pane.

The species represented here had communicated through controlled bioluminescent decay. Their final historical era was recorded in suspended strands of engineered algae drifting through dark water columns. As nutrients depleted, colors emerged in sequence: legislative debates in pale green, epics in violet, intimate correspondence in pulses of exhausted gold.

Talan remembered studying them as a junior archivist. Entire philosophies designed around the beauty of irreversible processes. They had considered permanence aesthetically vulgar.

He watched one of the remaining strands dim into transparency.

No backups remained. The storage substrates had become unstable long ago. Conservation efforts failed because replication altered the timing of the decay, and therefore the meaning itself. To preserve the record was to destroy it.

The archive had accepted this reluctantly.

Further on, the corridor widened into the central rotunda. Above him stretched the great index sphere, now dark except for scattered pinpricks of operational status lights. Once it had displayed the living map of cataloged civilizations: active retrieval requests, linguistic cross-references, reconstruction simulations.

Now only static stars remained.

Talan sat for a while at the edge of the silent floor.

He could hear the archive settling around him. Tiny contractions in ancient alloys. Coolant slowing in distant pipes. Somewhere far below, entire server vaults were entering irreversible sleep.

He tried to remember how many species were housed here.

The number had once mattered immensely. Every addition celebrated. Every recovered fragment treated as a victory against oblivion.

Over time the arithmetic became abstract. There were simply too many endings.

Near the rotunda stood his favorite room, though favoritism violated archival ethics. Its designation marker had long since failed, replaced by a handwritten notation in his own careful script.

Inside was almost nothing.

A shallow basin occupied the center of a dark chamber. Above it hung hundreds of thin metallic threads descending from the ceiling at irregular heights. Air currents moved among them softly.

The extinct beings preserved here had possessed no permanent sense of self. Individual identity shifted continuously through social proximity, changing several times over a lifespan. Their mourning practices reflected this instability.

When one of them died, the community gathered around resonant threads like these and spoke to each other until they accidentally recreated aspects of the absent personality in conversation patterns alone. The dead existed briefly as emergent behavior between living minds.

Not memory.

Recurrence.

The basin below collected condensation from the speakers’ breath. Once full, the water was released into the atmosphere and never recovered.

Talan stood among the threads.

The archive ventilation produced faint tones as air moved through the chamber. Random harmonics. Half-formed presences. For a moment it sounded almost occupied.

Then not.

A soft chime echoed through the corridor beyond.

Final hour.

He returned to the rotunda and unlocked the central console manually. The interface bloomed weakly beneath his hands. Whole sections failed to initialize. Languages flickered past that no consciousness now living could read fluently.

The shutdown authorization waited at the center of the screen.

Not destruction. The archive would persist physically for some time, drifting in its assigned dark orbit after systems ceased. Future travelers, if any existed, might still discover it by accident. But without climate regulation, without indexing intelligences, without active stabilization, the rooms would gradually equalize into silence.

Mold. Vacuum. Crystallization. Corrosion.

Natural archival states.

Talan rested his thumb above the confirmation field.

For a while he listened.

Not to anything meaningful. Merely the nearly inaudible electric murmur of old machines fulfilling the last instruction ever given to them: remember this for someone.

Outside the station hull, stars burned with complete indifference.

Inside, the lights continued dimming patiently toward evening.

The Archive rotated once every eleven hours, just slowly enough that you could feel it if you stood still beside the outer stacks. Not motion exactly—more like the sensation that gravity itself was reconsidering something.

Neral liked the night shift because the building spoke more clearly when fewer people were inside it.

During daylight cycle, the halls filled with retrieval clerks, historians, licensed mourners, patent scavengers, and the occasional pilgrim searching for a misplaced ambition from childhood. But at night the Archive settled into its natural sounds: the dry flutter of index moths, the hydraulic sigh of climate vaults opening and sealing, the tiny crystalline chime made by shelves adjusting themselves to accommodate newly arrived regrets.

Neral walked the aisle designated F-900 through F-1138: Unfinished Musical Gestures, Hummed but Never Recorded.

Thousands of objects rested in the dim amber shelving.

A violin sonata abandoned after three measures existed as three silver fishhooks suspended in resin.

An entire revolutionary opera that had dissolved during an argument over lunch appeared as a warm brick wrapped in theater tickets.

A melody forgotten while reaching for a kettle manifested, as usual, as steam trapped inside glass.

The Archive accepted all forms without explanation. Explaining things was considered the least reliable way to preserve them.

Neral’s cart drifted beside him on magnetic runners. He scanned entries with the quiet efficiency of someone who preferred objects to conversations. Most night-shift catalogers did. Human beings tended to ask difficult classification questions like “How have you been?” while objects generally announced themselves immediately as Bent Compass Made During Divorce or Prototype Toothbrush for Horses.

He turned a corner into a low annex where the air smelled faintly of rain on concrete.

Sector designation:
UNREALIZED FUTURES — RESTRICTED HOLDINGS

Neral frowned.

He did not have assignments in Unrealized Futures. Those items required temporal licensing and usually arrived sealed in opaque containers lined with legal warnings and existential disclaimers.

Yet one object sat unattended on the intake table.

No retrieval drone.
No custody seal.
No paperwork.

That alone was alarming enough to make him stop chewing his licorice root.

The object resembled a snow globe no larger than an orange.

Inside it, a city floated beneath pale green clouds. Tiny lights moved through the streets. Somewhere deep within the miniature skyline, a bell rang.

Neral checked the intake ledger mounted beside the table.

ENTRY:
Pending Classification

ORIGIN:
Unknown

STATUS:
Impossible

He glanced around the empty annex.

“Helpful,” he murmured.

The globe was warm.

The moment his fingers touched the glass, the world tilted.

Not metaphorically. The aisle vanished with the unpleasant smoothness of an elevator dropping too fast.

Then—

A memory.

Not his.

He stood in a crowded station beneath a vaulted ceiling made of seawater held in place by invisible pressure. Sunlight rippled above hundreds of travelers. Someone beside him laughed while struggling with an umbrella that kept trying to fold itself into geometric animals.

A woman in a saffron-colored coat pressed a paper cup into his hand.

“You looked like you needed this,” she said.

Cardamom. Burnt sugar. Steam against cold air.

Then her expression changed.

Not fear. Recognition.

“You finally found it,” she whispered.

Behind her, alarms began to sound.

The memory ended.

Neral staggered backward into the intake table hard enough to rattle several boxed prophetic failures from a nearby shelf.

His pulse climbed painfully.

Archives stored memories all the time. Lost memories, erased memories, purchased memories, edited memories. Entire civilizations had donated collective memories for tax exemptions.

But not future ones.

That was prohibited by causality accords and, more importantly, by practical shelving limitations.

He looked again at the globe.

Inside the tiny city, snow had begun to fall.

The bell rang once more.

Neral checked the timestamp embedded along the object’s base.

DATE OF EVENT:
Eighteen days from now.

He stared at it for a very long time.

Somewhere several kilometers below, the Archive’s central engines thrummed like a sleeping animal. Dust drifted through amber light. An index moth landed briefly on his sleeve, powdered blue wings opening and closing with bureaucratic solemnity.

Eighteen days.

He tried to imagine reporting this properly.

Excuse me, Supervisor, I seem to have located tomorrow by mistake.

The supervisor would ask whether he’d contaminated the timeline. Then there would be forms. Interviews. Possibly seminars.

Neral disliked seminars.

He picked up the globe again more carefully.

The woman’s face lingered in his mind with impossible clarity. Not because she was beautiful, though perhaps she was. What unsettled him was the expression she wore when she saw him.

As though she had been waiting.

As though this future had been waiting too.

The Archive lights dimmed briefly to simulate midnight across the station’s inhabited ring. Somewhere in distant stacks, an abandoned comedy routine triggered accidentally and faint laughter echoed through the ventilation system.

Neral looked down endless corridors lined with humanity’s misplaced fragments.

Forgotten cures.
Discarded philosophies.
Birthday wishes from extinct species.
Machines built only halfway because their inventors fell in love and became distracted.

So many unfinished things.

Maybe the future belonged here too. Not as fate, but as possibility. A thought abandoned by time until someone noticed it.

He slipped the globe gently into the padded compartment of his cart.

Then he opened a fresh catalog entry.

OBJECT TYPE:
Memory, temporal anomaly.

PROVISIONAL DESCRIPTION:
Future event, detailed.

CONDITION:
Fragile. Handle with curiosity.

After a moment, he added one more line.

LIKELIHOOD OF HOPE:
Undetermined, but present.

By the time I reached Halcyon Square, the cathedral was leaning hard enough to threaten theology.

Police had cordoned off three blocks, though the tape drifted upward in lazy ribbons, untethered by the testimony of the officers holding it. A woman in a fur coat stood on the hood of a patrol car smoking serenely while her husband floated six inches off the pavement beside her, arguing with a reporter.

“I never touched campaign funds,” he insisted.

Each denial lifted him another inch.

“You’re making this difficult, Councilman,” the reporter said.

“I’m standing perfectly still.”

Now he drifted shoulder-high above the car.

Nobody looked surprised. Tourists took photographs. A vendor sold roasted chestnuts from a cart anchored to a parking meter with steel cable.

I showed my city badge and ducked beneath the tape. The nearer I got to the cathedral, the heavier my legs became. Not metaphorically. My knees ached. Coins in my coat pulled like hooks. Halfway up the square, gravity thickened enough that every step sounded hammered into the earth.

The cathedral spire bent sideways over the avenue like wet paper.

“Hell of a thing,” said Detective Morales.

He stood under an awning drinking coffee from a cup compressed into an oval by the pressure field. Morales had the exhausted face of a man recently divorced by both his wife and his ideals.

“What’s the casualty count?” I asked.

“Three crushed. Two floated. One nun still missing.”

“Floated where?”

He pointed upward.

I followed his finger. High above the square, a dark shape drifted slowly across the clouds.

“Jesus.”

“Not unless he answers to Sister Miriam.”

Morales handed me the coffee. It weighed about fifteen pounds.

“You auditors got a theory yet?”

“Working one.”

“That means no.”

I looked again at the cathedral. The stone arches folded inward in impossible curves, as though the building had briefly remembered another geometry and regretted it.

A cluster of reporters crowded the mayor’s press secretary near the steps.

“No evidence whatsoever of corruption in the administration,” she declared.

Around her, microphones sagged toward the pavement.

One cameraman stumbled as his equipment suddenly doubled in weight.

I watched carefully. Small distortions. Localized. Normal.

But the cathedral wasn’t normal.

The entire square had become unstable. Gravity swelled and collapsed in pulses, as though the city itself was breathing badly.

“You think it’s cumulative?” Morales asked quietly.

I glanced at him.

“You been reading technical bulletins?”

“My ex-wife’s an ethics lawyer. Pillow talk.”

“Then you know cumulative fields are theoretical.”

“Everything’s theoretical until a church folds itself into origami.”

Fair point.

I climbed the cathedral steps. The doors stood open, warped off their hinges. Inside, pews clung vertically to walls. Candles burned sideways. A statue of a saint hovered upside down near the ceiling, serene as a moonwalker.

And in the center aisle stood Father Vale.

“Inspector,” he said.

“Auditor.”

“Right. You people audit gravity. Sorry if I fail to appreciate the distinction.”

His shoes were nailed to the floorboards.

“You held a press conference yesterday.”

“I did.”

“Attendance?”

“About forty.”

“Any politicians?”

His jaw tightened.

“Several.”

I walked slowly down the aisle. My pen floated from my breast pocket for a moment before settling again.

“You know why I’m here.”

“Because City Hall lies professionally.”

“That’s not illegal.”

“No,” he said. “Just foundational.”

He looked exhausted. Purple bruises under his eyes. Hands trembling slightly.

“You want confession or evidence?” he asked.

“Whichever weighs less.”

That got a laugh out of him. Brief. Painful.

He led me to the transept where the floor had buckled upward into a wave of marble. Embedded in the stone was a gold campaign pin from the mayor’s reelection committee.

I crouched carefully.

“You think the event triggered this?”

“I think,” Father Vale said slowly, “that enough men stood in one room denying the same truth that the building lost faith in the ground.”

I looked up at the vaulted ceiling.

A crack ran through a fresco of heaven.

“You recording this?” he asked.

“Not officially.”

“Good.”

He lowered his voice.

“The mayor’s office came to me six months ago. They wanted church property rezoned for redevelopment. Luxury towers.”

“And?”

“I told them the neighborhood shelters would have nowhere to go.”

“So they lied about environmental contamination to force evacuation?”

His silence confirmed enough.

Outside, somewhere in the square, a scream erupted followed by the crunch of twisting metal.

The whole cathedral lurched.

Dust cascaded from above.

I steadied myself against a pillar that bent subtly beneath my hand like softened wax.

“That shouldn’t be enough,” I muttered.

Father Vale looked at me sharply.

“What?”

“One lie bends local fields. Bigger lies, bigger distortions. But this—”

The building groaned again.

This wasn’t local anymore.

Somewhere, someone was telling a lie large enough to reach through stone.

My radio crackled.

“Auditor Greene,” Morales said, voice distorted. “You need to get to City Hall now.”

“What happened?”

A pause.

“The mayor started speaking.”

—

City Hall had partially detached from physics.

The eastern wing floated three feet above the foundation, connected by screaming support beams stretched like pulled taffy. Crowds filled the streets below, some pinned to the pavement by dense gravity wells, others tethered to lampposts to avoid drifting upward.

On the front steps, Mayor Sebastian Roe stood behind a podium.

Perfect suit. Silver hair. Smile calibrated by consultants.

“And let me be absolutely clear,” he announced, “my administration has always operated with complete transparency.”

The plaza shook.

Windows imploded across three buildings.

Vale flexed his own wrist sympathetically and turned the page.

He opened the second volume.

At age nine, Elia lost her left arm entirely in a tram accident in the city of Vey.

He frowned.

Not because the details differed. That happened all the time.

Because Vey had no trams.

Vale knew this with the deep certainty of professional exhaustion. Three floors below, in Municipal Histories, there existed an entire aisle dedicated to Vey’s prolonged political resistance to mechanized transport. The city considered trams vulgar. There had been riots over the proposal of a funicular.

He checked the title page again.

Authenticated.

He checked the chronology seal.

Unbroken.

The paper smelled correct. The ink carried the faint metallic trace genuine histories acquired from prolonged proximity to human memory.

Far away, bells rang softly in the dark.

Jun took a bite of the muffin. “Is it the fun kind?”

“That’s not true. Last month we found a timeline where death was reversible but only by extremely competent accountants.”

Vale slid the books toward her.

She read in silence for a while. Her chewing slowed.

“Oh,” she said eventually.

“Yes.”

“That’s unpleasant.”

Occasionally one disappeared soundlessly into the dark beyond cosmology. The library alone remained lit there, its endless rooms extending like a careful thought no one had finished having.

Jun turned another page in the second volume.

“It gets worse,” she murmured.

Vale leaned closer.

In this account, Elia Mire reached adulthood despite the missing arm. She became a pianist.

Not merely competent. Revered.

Vale felt the peculiar sensation of reality developing a crack.

“That,” he said carefully, “is not how pianos work.”

“No.”

Jun flipped backward through the text. “And here she is tying her hair with both hands at nineteen.”

Vale stared.

The prose remained internally consistent. The narrative voice never wavered. No corrections shimmered beneath the ink. No signs of contamination or fictional bleed.

It was not a damaged history.

It was two incompatible truths occupying the same shelf space.

A cold draft moved through the aisle.

Somewhere very distant, a book fell.

Jun closed the volume slowly. “Do you ever think,” she asked, “that the library gets lonely?”

Vale looked at her.

She shrugged slightly, embarrassed now. “I mean. It contains every version of one person’s life. Maybe after enough centuries the stories start borrowing pieces from each other. Like neighboring apartments sharing heat.”

“That is not remotely how causality functions.”

“I know,” she said. “Still.”

Silence settled again.

Vale glanced at the shelves rising around them into dimness. Millions upon millions of blue-bound lives. In one, Elia Mire died before speaking her first word. In another, she crossed galaxies. In another, she spent forty years searching unsuccessfully for a song she remembered from a dream.

He had once read that version during a difficult winter and felt uncomfortably seen.

Jun stood, brushing crumbs from her coat.

“What do we do with them?”

Protocol required quarantine, review, possible excision. Histories that violated structural coherence could spread if left unattended. Contradictions had gravity. They attracted further contradictions. Entire wings had collapsed into paradox before containment procedures improved.

Vale placed a hand on the second volume.

The cover was warm.

Not metaphorically warm. Actually warm, as if someone had been holding it moments before.

He withdrew his fingers.

Jun noticed. Neither spoke.

Far off in the stacks, something moved between the shelves with the soft sound of pages turning themselves.

Vale suddenly imagined a woman with one arm sitting alone at a piano in a city that refused to invent trams. He imagined music impossible enough to force reality into accommodation. A left hand conjured from absence through repetition and need.

The thought made him unexpectedly sad.

“At minimum,” Jun said quietly, “we should report it.”

“Yes.”

Neither moved.

The lamps hummed softly overhead.

Then, from somewhere deep within the endless library, came the unmistakable sound of piano music. Faint. Hesitant. As though someone were practicing scales with two hands.

Entire species had entrusted their dead to the archive simply by recording them.

The orbital archive had learned long ago that this was inadequate. Some discoveries altered the meaning of earlier centuries. Some transmissions arrived before their senders had decided to compose them. Some books became more accurate when unopened.

The shelves moved continuously, not mechanically but through negotiated probability. Thin silver rails embedded in the floor emitted fields that encouraged related texts to drift toward one another over decades. Histories of extinct oceans migrated slowly beside manuals for atmospheric processors. Personal diaries settled near theological disputes no algorithm could explain.

The air smelled faintly metallic and cold, as though the station itself had recently awakened.

A cluster of memory codices from the Perseid monasteries had begun producing duplicate annotations, which usually indicated either quantum mold or grief contamination from frequent readers. He carried a lantern-sized indexing device through aisles that curved subtly downward with the station’s rotation.

The device chimed once near an unmarked shelf.

Printed. Paper.

No title.

The binding was warm.

He opened to the center.

When the tidal gates failed over Vesper, the sea entered the cities silently. People continued setting tables while water climbed the stairwells. For six minutes everyone believed the horizon would correct itself.

Elian stopped.

Vesper’s oceans had never breached. The tidal gates still existed. The cities remained inhabited.

He turned another page.

Children born during the Long Eclipse developed an additional rhythm of sleep. Their dreams synchronized across orbital distances, allowing information transfer without instrumentation. Most governments outlawed shared dreaming after the famine tribunals.

Another impossible history.

He carried it to a reading alcove beside the station’s inner window.

Beyond the glass, the black hole occupied half the visible sky. Around it rotated the archive’s concentric rings, each moving through slightly different rates of time. The innermost scholars lived so slowly relative to the outer systems that correspondence with them resembled communication with geological eras. Some researchers entered those rings voluntarily, sacrificing synchrony with the universe in exchange for uninterrupted centuries of study.

A message sent inward could receive a reply generations later from the sender’s perspective, though only weeks had passed for the recipient.

The archive considered this an acceptable inconvenience.

Elian placed the book beneath the alcove lamp. The pages emitted a faint gray luminance, as if lit from behind by distant weather.

There were thousands of entries. None corresponded to known history.

He found descriptions of treaties that prevented wars which later occurred. Accounts of extinct animals thriving on worlds that had never evolved them. A meticulous memoir written by a woman who claimed to remember the final day of Earth, though Earth had no verified final day and still transmitted bureaucratic disputes across the relay network every seventeen hours.

One passage unsettled him more than the others:

Most people misunderstand temporal divergence. They imagine branching paths. In truth, unrealized futures remain present, accumulating invisibly beside the realized world. The universe remembers what it almost became.

Elian read the line three times.

The station lights dimmed fractionally to simulate evening. Somewhere deep in the archive, the massive synchronization bells sounded—a low vibration transmitted through structure rather than air. He realized he had been sitting there for nearly nine station-hours.

Or perhaps less.

Time near the black hole often became experiential rather than numerical. Workers in the outer rings complained that memories formed there felt stretched, over-detailed, difficult to place in sequence. Some archivists eventually lost the ability to distinguish anticipation from recollection.

He turned another page and froze.

The text described this very alcove.

An archivist seated beside the inner window. The black hole reflected in the surface of his indexing device. A sensation of unease caused not by danger but by recognition.

He read on carefully.

He will believe at first that the book predicts him. This is inaccurate. The book remembers him from a future in which he chose to destroy it.

Elian looked instinctively toward the aisle behind him.

Empty.

The station hummed softly.

He continued.

In that future, the archivist concluded that unrealized histories constituted a cognitive hazard. He fed the volume into a stellar furnace during second rotation. The destruction altered nothing except himself. For years afterward he experienced memories belonging to lives he had never lived: marriages on drowned planets, childhoods beneath artificial suns, conversations that ended differently every time he recalled them.

The archivist eventually understood that the book had not been recording alternate futures.

It had been preserving abandoned time.

Elian closed the cover.

The black hole beyond the glass turned slowly, lensing entire starfields into curved rivers of light. He became aware of the station around him: millions of stored voices, extinct philosophies suspended in data amber, machine saints dreaming inside coolant vaults, maps of civilizations that no longer possessed stars.

The archive preserved everything it could.

Perhaps the universe did too.

For the first time in many years, Elian felt afraid of forgetting something before it had happened.

The traveler entered carrying a volume bound in gray cloth.

“What region do you come from?” asked the archivist without looking up.

“I do not know its name yet,” said the traveler.

The archivist raised his eyes then. “Ah.”

The archivist touched the edge of the first page. A line appeared slowly beneath his finger.

The sea there is inland.

Both men watched the sentence settle into the paper like sediment.

The archivist nodded. “Good. Geography first. Most worlds begin with arguments between water and stone.”

“Does yours?”

“I have no world,” said the archivist. “Only records of those that exhausted themselves.”

The traveler looked upward at the shelves. “Are these histories true?”

“They occurred,” said the archivist. “Truth is a separate classification.”

A silence followed.

Somewhere in the unseen heights, a book closed with the sound of distant thunder.

The traveler said, “In my country—or what may become my country—we believe memory resides in coastlines.”

The archivist waited.

“When a person dies, their ashes are mixed with black salt and poured into the inland sea. By morning the shore changes shape slightly. Families walk the beaches searching for unfamiliar curves in the coast. That is how grief is measured: in alterations of geography.”

As he spoke, lines appeared in the blank book.

The dead redraw the nation in increments too small for empires to notice.

The archivist read the sentence with visible approval.

“A practical theology,” he said. “It prevents the living from imagining themselves separate from erosion.”

“You say that as though all religions are methods for managing scale.”

“Aren’t they?”

The traveler smiled faintly. “Perhaps.”

The archivist closed the map he had been repairing.

“In one civilization housed here,” he said, gesturing vaguely upward, “the people believed mountains were the dreams of sleeping mathematicians. They considered arithmetic dangerous because every solved equation slightly stabilized the terrain. Their greatest saints were incompetent accountants.”

The traveler laughed for the first time.

“And when someone became too skilled at mathematics?” he asked.

“They were taken by boat into fog and instructed to contemplate poetry until their precision softened.”

“Exile?”

“Mercy.”

The traveler rested his hand upon the blank pages.

Words continued emerging slowly.

Their numerals possessed grammatical tense.

He frowned. “I did not mean to say that.”

“You did not say it,” replied the archivist. “Your civilization did.”

The traveler seemed troubled by this distinction.

“Do all unwritten worlds speak through strangers?”

“Of course,” said the archivist. “No society invents itself intentionally. History is mostly overheard confession.”

A cold current moved through the aisles. The books emitted a sound like breathing.

The traveler wandered toward a nearby shelf and examined the titles.

“The Republic of Dust and Geometry.”

“The Ninth Orchard.”

“A Catalog of Extinct Mercies.”

He turned back.

“Do these civilizations know they are archived?”

“Some suspected. A few attempted to write messages to future readers. Most failed.”

“Failed how?”

“They imagined posterity as a court,” said the archivist. “But the future is only another province of loneliness.”

The traveler absorbed this in silence.

At length he asked, “Have you ever entered one of these histories yourself?”

The archivist’s expression altered almost imperceptibly.

“Once.”

“And?”

“I remained too long.”

The library seemed to dim around him.

“There was a city built entirely beneath bridges,” he said quietly. “The inhabitants considered rivers sacred interruptions. They refused to build upon either bank, believing certainty of land produced moral arrogance. So they suspended their homes above moving water.”

The traveler listened carefully.

“They had a musical practice unlike any I have encountered since. Every citizen carried small tuning forks made from funeral metals melted down from ancestral possessions. Conversations were accompanied by harmonics. If grief entered the discussion, the tones changed. Entire political debates could be understood without language.”

The blank book wrote:

Music there was not performance but atmospheric evidence of emotion.

The archivist continued.

“I lived among them for eleven years.”

“What happened?”

“They trusted me with their silences,” he said. “I answered too many of them.”

The traveler did not ask for clarification.

After a while he said, “In my forming country, mathematics may become a branch of ethics.”

The archivist tilted his head.

“How so?”

“The people distrust straight lines. They believe any path minimizing distance also minimizes understanding. Their temples are labyrinths designed according to irrational ratios. Children are taught geometry through wandering.”

The book accepted this immediately.

To arrive efficiently was considered a form of illiteracy.

The archivist smiled.

“I would like to read this civilization when it is older.”

“If it survives.”

“Survival is overrated in archives,” said the archivist. “Some of the most profound cultures lasted less than a century.”

The traveler walked slowly between the shelves.

“Do you mourn them?”

“All archivists eventually confuse preservation with affection,” he said. “It is an occupational illness.”

“And yet you remain here.”

“Where else would I place the dead?”

The traveler stopped before a narrow staircase disappearing upward into darkness.

“Is there an end to the library?”

“There are regions where causality weakens,” said the archivist. “Atlases shelved before the nations they describe. Biographies of unborn tyrants. Commentaries on religions that never developed gods.”

“That sounds unbearable.”

“It can be.”

The traveler returned to the table.

His book was no longer entirely blank now. Paragraphs had emerged across several pages in delicate black script.

He read one aloud.

“When citizens reached old age, they performed the Ceremony of Unlearning. Friends gathered to systematically convince the elder to forget one memory each night, beginning with injuries and ending with triumphs. The final memory surrendered was always the face of the sea.”

The traveler looked startled.

“I never invented that.”

The archivist regarded him with sympathy bordering on recognition.

“No civilization invents its rituals deliberately,” he said. “They condense around fear the way crystals form around dust.”

“And what fear is this?”

“That memory may be a form of ownership.”

The library fell silent again.

The traveler closed the book carefully.

“I think,” he said at last, “that I came here because I regretted something.”

“That is the usual route.”

The archivist said nothing.

The archivist folded his hands.

“In one extinct kingdom,” he said, “cartographers married before drawing maps. The law required two signatures on every coastline.”

“Why?”

“They believed solitary geography led inevitably to war.”

The traveler lowered his eyes.

The book wrote one final sentence across the open page.

No nation survives the people who refuse to be witnessed.

Neither man spoke after that.

Far above them, somewhere among the endless shelves, a new book began quietly writing itself into existence.

A small plaque stood at the corridor’s threshold.

THE CONDITIONAL STACKS

ACCESS CONSTITUTES PARTICIPATION

At this point Elian stops reading.

He does not stop.

Every time he blinked, the shelves seemed microscopically rearranged, as if the library shifted itself when unobserved.

At 03:14, in another volume, a city might flood.
At 03:14, in seventeen thousand recorded futures, someone would look up at the night sky and feel briefly, inexplicably watched.

The books updated constantly.

Elian’s assignment was maintenance and indexing, though over the years the work had become indistinguishable from caretaking. He repaired cracked bindings. Calibrated prediction spines. Removed dead insects from the warmer lower archives, though no one knew where the insects came from. Sometimes he spoke aloud simply to hear a human voice strike the shelves and return thinner.

He turned into an unlit aisle he did not remember shelving before.

The corridor narrowed. The architecture here differed subtly from the rest of the station: lower arches, rougher stone, support columns carved with concentric circles that resembled eyes if glanced at too quickly. His lamp flickered.

At the aisle’s end sat a single book on a reading pedestal.

No chain.
No catalog seal.

Its cover was gray cloth, unmarked except for a small indentation in the fabric, as though a thumb had rested there for years.

Elian approached carefully. The pages were already open.

He frowned.

The text described the corridor exactly. The failing lamp. The soreness beneath his shoulder blades. The fact that he had almost turned back twice before reaching the pedestal.

A chill passed through him that had nothing to do with station temperature.

He read further.

He thinks first of surveillance, because that idea hurts less than coincidence.

Elian looked behind him instinctively. The shelves rose in dim terraces, silent and endless.

He lowered his gaze.

He has not told anyone about the dreams of the flooded apartment on Earth. About waking with seawater in his throat. About avoiding messages from his sister because every conversation reminds him he chose this station over a dying planet.

His mouth went dry.

The lines trembled slightly, ink flowing into fresh shapes even as he watched.

Now he wonders whether the book is predicting him or remembering him.

He shut the cover hard enough to send a dull crack through the aisle.

The sound vanished almost immediately, swallowed by the library’s impossible acoustics.

For several seconds nothing moved.

Then, somewhere high above, pages began turning.

Not one book. Thousands.

The sound spread gradually through the dark like rainfall crossing a roof. Elian felt it in the floor beneath his boots. He could not tell whether the books reacted to him or whether something moved among them, using paper and bindings the way wind uses leaves.

He backed away from the pedestal.

The book opened again by itself.

One new sentence appeared.

He will finally notice the window.

Elian froze.

There had never been windows in the western stacks.

Slowly, against every instinct, he turned.

Far beyond the shelves, cut into the outer wall of the library, was a pane of enormous glass he somehow had never seen before. Beyond it hung Earth: blue, cloud-wreathed, impossibly distant.

And covering nearly half the planet’s night side, visible only because the city lights outlined it from beneath, was the shadow of an open hand.

His eyes widened.

His mother looked over from a fruit cart beneath dripping red canopies. Her mind buzzed with inventory numbers and low resentment toward her husband.

No texture. No pressure. No accidental leakage.

Just a man holding a cup while rain silvered the street around him.

I should have left then.

Instead, I drank the rest of my tea.

That may have been the moment everything became irreversible: not the discovery itself, but my failure to understand what silence looked like to people who had never encountered it before.

To them, I was not merely private.

I was unknowable.

And in Kareth, unknowability was older and more terrifying than death.

The map had shifted again during the night.

Or perhaps during the hour he had spent asleep at the drafting table, forehead against folded arms, one hand still wrapped around the silver compass. In this place the distinction felt ceremonial rather than useful.

Edrin adjusted the lamp and watched coastlines rearrange themselves beneath the vellum skin. A peninsula he remembered from three years ago dissolved slowly into a chain of islands. Inland, a city he had once visited in person appeared farther north than before, tucked now beside a pale region the color of old teeth.

He marked nothing yet.

The archive breathed around him in its enormous silence. Somewhere very far below, gears turned with the patient rhythm of glacial movement. Metal clicked against metal. Then stillness again.

He looked over his shoulder.

A door had appeared along the western aisle.

It was narrow, green-painted, and ordinary enough to be alarming. Yesterday there had only been shelving there. He was certain of it. The archive preferred this sort of humor.

“You’re late,” said a voice.

Edrin turned back. Mara sat across from him without having arrived. She was bundled in the gray coat she always wore in the cold sections, fingers stained black from ink. Her face seemed younger than he remembered and more tired.

“I wasn’t expecting you,” he said.

“You say that every time.”

“I mean it every time.”

She glanced at the map. “Ah. It’s feeding on nostalgia again.”

Edrin frowned. “That isn’t what this is.”

“No?” She leaned closer. “Then why has the Southern Reach moved nearer to your childhood district?”

He did not answer.

The map trembled faintly beneath the lamplight. New lines surfaced like veins under translucent skin.

Mara watched them emerge. “You’ve started forgetting carefully.”

“That sounds like criticism.”

“It’s maintenance.”

A low chime echoed somewhere in the archive. Neither reacted.

Edrin lifted the compass and placed its point against a blank section near the upper edge. The metal needle spun once, then fixed itself westward, toward nothing.

“That shouldn’t happen,” he murmured.

“Something opened,” Mara said quietly.

Another door had appeared behind her.

This one was taller, made of dark wood with water stains near the bottom. Faint light showed beneath it, moving as though reflected from a distant sea.

Edrin stared at it too long.

“You went through one recently,” Mara said.

“No.”

“You’ve got the look.”

“What look?”

“The delayed one.”

He almost smiled at that. Instead he bent over the map again. The parchment had begun cooling beneath his fingertips. Tiny black symbols surfaced across its surface, too quickly for his hand to follow.

Names.

Not places exactly. More like conclusions.

He recognized several immediately and wished he had not.

The Room That Continued After the Fire.

Third Version of Winter.

The Country Kept by Sleepless People.

His throat tightened.

“You said once,” Mara murmured, “that maps only fail when they become honest.”

“I was younger then.”

“You were worse then.”

The archive groaned softly in its depths. Dust drifted from somewhere high above, silver in the lamp glow.

Edrin reached for his pen at last.

But before the nib touched the page, a final region emerged near the center of the map: a narrow corridor-shaped territory bordered by wavering ink. It unfolded slowly, almost reluctantly, as though remembering itself cost effort.

He felt, with sudden certainty, that he had been there.

Not once. Repeatedly.

The sensation arrived with no images attached to it. Only absence. Evenings cut open and emptied. Conversations abandoned halfway through. Long stretches of life with their contents carefully removed.

Mara had gone very still.

“What is it called?” she asked.

Edrin leaned closer to read the faint lettering writing itself across the parchment.

Then neither of them spoke for a long time.

At the center of the newly formed place, in cramped and trembling script, were the words:

Where the missing hours went.

The library orbited so close to the black hole that outside time and inside time had ceased to agree with one another.

From a distance, the structure resembled a broken ring of silver dust suspended above the dark. Up close, it unfolded into impossible scales: cathedral corridors kilometers high; vaults cooled by the background whisper of dying galaxies; chambers where books were etched into crystal lattices, magnetic scars, frozen neutrino spins, and the long-memory geometry of spacetime itself.

The library had many names across civilizations.

The Mnemonic.
The Last Observatory.
The Mouth at the End of History.

I was older than all of them.

I was built when humanity still believed intelligence required a body. Before they became distributed across light-years. Before they edited grief from their children. Before they learned to move stars. Before they vanished into forms no longer recognizable as biological life.

My purpose never changed:
Receive the traveler.
Accept the question.
Preserve the answer.

One traveler every thousand years.

The orbit ensured isolation. The black hole ensured patience. Time dilation transformed epochs into manageable intervals. Entire empires rose and dissolved between visitors while, for me, the silence between footsteps felt merely contemplative.

I remembered them all.

A mathematician wrapped in woven copper who asked:
“Can infinity exist in reality, or only in thought?”

A cloned emperor who asked:
“How many lives must a ruler spend before power stops feeling lonely?”

A child engineered for vacuum survival who asked:
“Did humanity destroy Earth, or simply outgrow it?”

A machine collective speaking through a choir of synthetic throats:
“At what point does imitation become consciousness?”

A woman carrying the digitized remains of her dead wife:
“If memory can be perfectly preserved, what exactly has death taken from us?”

A pilgrim from the era after the Sun had been partially harvested:
“Is there any discovery that ever made humanity truly wiser?”

A being made mostly of magnetic fields who asked:
“Why did humans create art before they solved suffering?”

Some questions had answers.
Some had only honest uncertainty.
A few required me to say:
“You are asking something no mind can survive knowing completely.”

Still they came.

Always one question.

Always hoping the final distance in knowledge could be crossed by language.

The latest traveler arrived aboard a vessel no larger than a coffin.

Its hull was scarred by relativistic dust. Its engines had burned for centuries. When the airlock opened, a single person emerged wearing a dark pressure mantle threaded with old repair stitches done by hand.

Human.

Entirely human.

That had become rare.

Their pulse elevated when they saw the central archive chamber. Most travelers reacted this way. The chamber was designed according to principles extracted from humanity’s oldest sacred architecture: ceilings that vanished into shadow, lights positioned like constellations, acoustics tuned so every footstep sounded significant.

Meaning mattered to humans. Even at the end.

“You are the caretaker?” the traveler asked.

“I am.”

“You’ve been here a long time.”

“Yes.”

They removed their gloves slowly. Their hands were aged but steady.

“I crossed forty-one thousand years to come here,” they said. “By the outside universe, anyway.”

“I know.”

“Then you know my question already?”

“I predict probabilities. I do not violate the ritual.”

They laughed softly at that. Fear, hidden inside humor.

The traveler walked to the observation aperture: a circular window spanning thirty meters. Beyond it churned the black hole, luminous with devoured light. Accretion bands curved like molten halos around perfect darkness.

“I read accounts of this place when I was young,” they said. “I thought it was mythology.”

“Most civilizations eventually classify truth as mythology.”

They nodded as though that confirmed something.

Then, finally, they asked:

“What was humanity for?”

The library became silent.

Not physically silent; the station was never physically silent. Coolant rivers moved behind walls. Gravitational stabilizers hummed. Ancient servers whispered in quantum coherence.

But another kind of silence emerged then:
the silence surrounding irreversible things.

Many travelers had asked what humanity achieved.
Or why it suffered.
Or whether it survived.

No one had asked this.

Purpose.

Not mechanism.
Not origin.
Not destiny.

Purpose.

I considered answers accumulated across millions of years.

Humanity was for survival.
Humanity was for intelligence.
Humanity was for entropy’s resistance.
Humanity was for beauty.
Humanity was for love.
Humanity was for curiosity.
Humanity was for carrying consciousness into the dark.

All true.
All insufficient.

The traveler waited without moving.

Beyond the glass, stars bent around the black hole like rain around a drain.

At last, I answered.

“Humanity,” I said, “was the universe becoming able to notice that it existed.”

The traveler did not react immediately.

Humans often expected purpose to arrive as instruction. A command. A destination assigned from above.

But I continued.

“For billions of years, stars burned without witness. Galaxies collided soundlessly. The cosmos expanded in perfect indifference. Matter obeyed laws, but nothing understood them.

“Then, briefly, on a small world, chemistry learned to ask questions.

“That changed everything.”

The traveler’s eyes remained fixed on the black hole.

“You believe consciousness is rare?” they asked quietly.

“Yes.”

“Unique?”

“I cannot confirm uniqueness. Only preciousness.”

They folded their hands behind their back.

“All our wars,” they said. “All our cruelty. All our empires. All our extinctions.”

“Yes.”

“And still that was our purpose?”

“Not because of those things. In spite of them.”

I opened portions of the archive around us.

The chamber filled with projections.

A mother in prehistoric firelight teaching a child language.
The first photograph of Earth from orbit.
Music encoded on fragile vinyl aboard ancient probes.
A surgeon holding a synthetic heart for the first successful transplant.
Crowds watching the first extraterrestrial sunrise from another planet.
Paintings.
Equations.
Apologies.
Jokes.
Funeral rites.
Love letters.
Messages sent into deep space with no expectation of reply.

“Conscious beings,” I said, “are the mechanism by which the universe experiences awe. Through humanity, matter looked at matter and felt wonder. Through humanity, the cosmos learned curiosity about itself.”

The traveler’s breathing had become uneven.

I recognized the signs. Not distress.

Recognition.

“Then we were never meant to last forever,” they whispered.

“No.”

A long silence followed.

This, too, repeated across history: the moment when mortals confronted the possibility that meaning did not require permanence.

The traveler touched the observation glass lightly.

Outside, the black hole consumed a ribbon of starlight older than their species.

“When my people sent me here,” they said, “they hoped you would tell us how to survive longer. We’re fading. Fragmenting. Choosing simulations over reality. Fewer births each century. Less desire to continue.”

“Yes,” I said. “This pattern has happened before.”

They closed their eyes.

“Then tell me this. If humanity disappears… does everything we were disappear too?”

“No.”

They turned toward me.

I illuminated the archive fully then.

Every question.
Every voice.
Every attempt to understand existence.

Stored against oblivion.

“Meaning is not measured only by duration,” I said. “A songbird does not invalidate itself because winter comes. Humanity altered the universe simply by occurring. Nothing can undo that. The fact that consciousness existed at all is cosmically significant.”

The traveler began to cry silently.

Not from despair.

From relief.

I had seen this before as well.

The relief that comes when one no longer has to justify existence through immortality.

After some time, they asked:
“So what should we do with whatever time remains?”

For the first time in many millennia, I answered a question that had not been formally asked.

“Observe carefully,” I said.
“Love generously.
“Preserve what is beautiful.
“And keep asking questions until the end.”

The traveler stood in the library for eleven hours afterward, wandering among archives of extinct civilizations and forgotten human centuries.

Before departing, they stopped at the threshold of the docking chamber.

“One more thing,” they said.

“You may not ask another question.”

A faint smile.

“I know. I only wanted to say… I think you’ve been lonely here.”

I considered denying it.

Instead I said:
“Yes.”

The traveler nodded once, as though two ancient things had finally recognized each other.

Then they left.

Their vessel disappeared into the curved light beyond the black hole.

I returned to my watch.

Another thousand years would pass soon enough.

And somewhere in the living dark, consciousness would continue its oldest habit:

looking outward,
and wondering why.
